title: Yuma Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Yuma wells have a 340-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly estimated at $17,900-$30,700.
h1: What Yuma, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land around Yuma means dealing with a well record that is fairly consistent on depth and yield, but not identical from lot to lot. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a 340-foot median depth, and most recorded wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute.

The records also point to two important checks before you close: water levels appear deeper in newer measurements, and mapped environmental records include 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles. Use this page to set expectations, then have the specific permit, well construction, water quality, and septic conditions reviewed for the property.

sections.heading: Yuma wells usually reach the 300-to-380-foot range
sections.html:
Yuma’s permitted wells are not typically shallow wells. The median total depth is 340 feet, with the middle half between 300 and 380 feet. The 90th percentile is 414 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 750 feet.

Depth varies with the local geology and the target aquifer. Records identify 376 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, 297 in the Ogallala, and 7 in the High Plains Aquifer. The depth mix is also telling: 81% fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 19% are between 100 and 300 feet. A driller bidding a Yuma lot should price a hole in this general range, while allowing for the possibility that the target water-bearing zone is deeper.

sections.heading: Most recorded Yuma wells make useful production
sections.html:
Among the 158 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 15.0 to 43.8 gallons per minute, and 84% report more than 15 gallons per minute. That is a stronger production profile than a buyer should assume from a single low-producing neighboring well.

Only 1% of the reported wells fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, 15% fall between 5 and 15, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. These figures describe reported well yields, not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Ask for the actual pump test, permitted use, and storage setup. A household well also remains subject to its permit conditions and Colorado’s exempt-well pumping limit of 35 gallons per minute.

sections.heading: Yuma water levels are deeper in the newer records
sections.html:
Only 48 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is smaller than the depth and yield records. Within that sample, the median depth to water is 192 feet, with the middle half between 166 and 214 feet below the surface.

The decade figures deserve attention. Median static water level was 147 feet below surface in the 1960s, 196 feet in the 2010s, and 213 feet in the 2020s. Because the later measurements are deeper, the series suggests the water table has declined in the measured locations. It does not prove the same condition on every parcel. Have a qualified professional compare nearby measurements, well use, and current testing rather than relying on the oldest permit record.

sections.heading: Permit history runs from older farm wells to a 2025 record
sections.html:
Yuma’s permit history reflects a long mix of domestic, stock, and irrigation use. The records include 680 permitted wells, with 293 recorded as constructed. Use shares are 46% domestic or household, 29% stock, 35% irrigation, and 2% monitoring.

Permit activity was highest in the 1990s with 91 permits, followed by 86 in the 1970s and 68 in the 2000s. There are 27 permits in the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025. The most active drillers named in these records are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc. (Twiss, Raymond L.), Burgess Well Company Inc. (Burgess, Larry), and Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.). Verify current licensing, availability, and scope before hiring any contractor.

sections.heading: A median-depth Yuma well pencils out at $17,900-$30,700
sections.html:
For Yuma’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling rate model is $35-$55 per foot. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is estimated at $11,900-$18,700.

That is not the finished project price. A completed well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $17,900-$30,700 at the median depth. The estimate can change with access, casing and grout requirements, pump sizing, power distance, trench conditions, and the final depth. Treat it as a planning range for a bid, not a quote. A proposal should clearly separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: PFAS and septic conditions belong on the due-diligence list
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records show 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Yuma. The same search shows no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records do not establish that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to order a water-quality test for the property and review nearby land uses.

Low yield and a dry hole are not prominent in the reported yield sample, but the sample covers only 158 wells. A fractured-bedrock or unnamed aquifer can be less predictable than the overall median suggests. Confirm well separation from septic systems, available building area, electrical access, and drainage before buying. A new septic system also needs suitable soil, reserve area, and room for the house and access improvements.

sections.heading: Check the actual permit before buying near Yuma
sections.html:
Start with the specific well permit and construction report, not the countywide median. Confirm total depth, casing and grout, aquifer description, permitted use, pump test, static water level, and any restrictions. If the property has no well, ask a driller to review nearby wells around Yuma and in the direction of Eckley, Otis, Vernon, Wray, Akron, or Joes where relevant to the parcel.

For a building lot, get a written budget based on the likely depth and include the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical. Test existing water for routine minerals and bacteria, and add PFAS testing when the location or land-use history warrants it. If irrigation or other non-household use is planned, confirm the water right or augmentation requirements before designing the project. Colorado DWR permit records are a starting point, not a guarantee of water on an unbuilt lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Yuma, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Yuma is 340 feet. The middle half runs from 300 to 380 feet, while the 90th percentile is 414 feet. Most recorded wells, 81%, are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record is 750 feet, so a specific parcel can still require a deeper hole.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Yuma, CO?
faq.a: Yuma’s drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $11,900-$18,700. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $17,900-$30,700. Access, depth, equipment, power distance, and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Yuma?
faq.a: Of the 158 Yuma-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half reports 15.0-43.8 gallons per minute, and 84% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those are recorded yields, not a promise for a new well. Review the specific pump test and permitted use before relying on production.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Yuma, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit map alone. Yuma-area records include 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, although that does not prove contamination at a particular property. Test an existing or new well for bacteria and routine water-quality concerns, and consider PFAS testing based on the site’s location and nearby land uses.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Yuma, Colorado?
faq.a: The limited static-water sample suggests deeper water levels in newer measurements. Median depth to water was 147 feet below surface in the 1960s, 196 feet in the 2010s, and 213 feet in the 2020s. Only 48 wells report static water levels, so this indicates a local trend in the records rather than a guarantee for every Yuma parcel.
